endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: If a contract is executed before a full AI governance review can be completed, document this with a defined timeline for completing the review and a process for contract amendment if needed.

endorsements.title: Responsible Use of AI in Healthcare (RUAIH) guidance
endorsements.issuer: The Joint Commission and Coalition for Health AI
endorsements.quote: To protect patient privacy and ensure consumer confidence, healthcare organizations must ensure the data privacy and the transparency of AI use to patients and staff.

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: In addition, the team should determine whether the developer team incorporates a method (e.g. Model Cards) to communicate to end users the fact that they are interacting with an AI.

endorsements.title: Principles for augmented intelligence development, deployment, and use
endorsements.quote: When AI is utilized in health care decision-making at the point of care, that use should be disclosed and documented to limit risks to, and mitigate inequities for, both patients and physicians, and to allow each to understand how decisions impacting patient care or access to care are made.

endorsements.title: Developing, purchasing, implementing and monitoring AI tools in radiology: practical considerations. A multi-society statement
endorsements.issuer: ACR, CAR, ESR, RANZCR, RSNA; Radiol Artif Intell 2024 (PMID 38251899, doi:10.1148/ryai.230513)
endorsements.quote: Autonomous AI should be designed to initiate actions that are transparent, identifiable, and discoverable.

evidence.title: Physician Ratings and Adoption of AI-Generated e-Consultation Advice: A Randomized Clinical Vignette Study
evidence.effect: AI vs human labeling: OR 1.18, 95% CI 0.51-2.75; p = 0.70.
evidence.quote: Labeling the advice as human- or GAI-generated did not significantly affect adoption of e-consult recommendations (OR 1.18, 95% CI 0.51-2.75; p = 0.70).

evidence.title: Optimistic and ambivalent attitudes toward clinical artificial intelligence
evidence.outcome: Staff awareness of whether AI tools are used in their workplace
evidence.effect: 24.6% reported using AI-based systems in clinical practice; 35.4% were uncertain whether such systems were used in their workplaces.
evidence.quote: Only 24.6% reported using AI-based systems in clinical practice, while 35.4% were uncertain whether such systems were used in their workplaces.

commentary.bottom_line: Five frameworks and guidance documents endorse telling staff which AI tools operate in their workflows, but the only test is one small vignette study, and it found no clear effect of labeling advice as AI-generated on physicians' adoption of e-consult recommendations (OR 1.18, 95% CI 0.51-2.75). A separate survey found that 35.4% of 260 staff in Türkiye were unsure whether AI was used in their workplace, which suggests the hazard exists.

perspectives.view: One simulated study of 44 physicians tests a form of AI disclosure, and its wide confidence interval (0.51-2.75) cannot exclude either meaningful increases or decreases in adoption. The study labels individual recommendations rather than testing an institutional policy, so it is indirect. Imprecision, indirectness, and single-study design place certainty at very low.

The survey shows that about one in three staff could not say whether AI systems were in use, so unrecognized reliance on AI output is plausible. That finding documents the problem. No study measured whether disclosure helps staff detect AI errors before they reach patients.

In the vignette study, knowing that a recommendation came from AI did not clearly change physicians' uptake (p = 0.70). The study took place offline, so it does not show whether disclosure survives in live workflows where AI features sit inside vendor software and may change after updates.

Neither study reports settings serving Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. The evidence therefore cannot show whether staff disclosure affects care differently for these groups, as the augmented intelligence principles intend when they cite mitigating inequities.

The endorsements rest on consensus rather than trial data. RUAIH frames staff transparency as a must, CHAI asks governance teams to confirm that developers disclose AI interaction, and the radiology multi-society statement asks that autonomous AI actions be identifiable and discoverable. None of these sources cites an outcome study.

commentary.research_gap: No study has tested an institutional policy that informs staff of embedded or third-party AI tools. Studies in live clinical and administrative workflows should measure staff awareness, appropriate reliance, override of incorrect outputs, and patient-level errors before and after such a policy is adopted.
commentary.underserved_note: Neither the test study, which enrolled 44 United States physicians in a simulation, nor the hazard survey from Türkiye included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Any effect of staff disclosure on care for these patients remains untested.
